title: India's Russian Oil Imports Hold Near Record Highs Despite Expired US Sanctions Waiver
excerpt: Indian refiners imported 2.45 million barrels per day of Russian crude in July, just below June's record 2.64 million bpd, as the Hormuz crisis reshapes global energy flows.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India imported 2.45 million barrels per day of Russian crude in July, near June's record high.
  • Russian oil now constitutes over 50% of India's total crude imports, up from 38% last year.
  • US sanctions waiver expired on June 17, yet Indian refiners continue to buy Russian oil.
  • Middle East oil imports dropped 27% in April-June due to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Surge in Import Bill (April-June)
Data from Kpler and Reuters
  • India imported 2.45 million barrels per day of Russian crude in July, near the record 2.64 million bpd set in June, according to Kpler data
  • Russian oil now accounts for over half of India's total crude imports, up from 38% a year ago
  • The US quietly let the waiver for Russian oil purchases expire on June 17, but Indian refiners have continued buying from non-sanctioned entities
  • Middle East oil imports fell 27% in the April-June quarter as the Strait of Hormuz blockade disrupted Gulf supplies

India's crude oil imports from Russia have remained close to all-time highs in July despite the expiry of a US Treasury waiver that had shielded purchases from sanctions, according to data from energy analytics firm Kpler, cited by multiple outlets.

Indian refiners imported an average of 2.45 million barrels per day (bpd) of Russian crude so far this month, not far off the record 2.64 million bpd recorded in June, when purchases surged 37.4% from the previous month, according to Reuters.

How the Hormuz Crisis Reshaped India's Oil Map

The sustained reliance on Russian crude is driven less by choice than by geopolitical necessity. India's oil imports from the Middle East fell 27% to 1.55 million bpd in the April-June quarter as the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that handles roughly a fifth of global oil supplies — was disrupted by the US-Israeli military campaign against Iran.

With Gulf supplies constrained, Indian refiners turned to Russia, which now accounts for roughly 41% of India's total crude imports, up from 38% a year earlier. Middle Eastern oil's share dropped to 31% from 41.4% over the same period, according to Reuters data.

"Russian crude imports rose to around 2.6 million barrels per day in June, accounting for more than 50% of India's crude imports, and have been steadily increasing since March."

— Sumit Ritolia, Lead Research Analyst, Kpler

The Waiver That Expired — and What Comes Next

The US Treasury quietly allowed its waiver for purchases of Russian oil already loaded on tankers to expire on June 17, according to OilPrice.com. Washington had extended the waiver multiple times since March, providing temporary legal cover for buyers including India.

Despite the lapse, Indian refiners have continued importing Russian crude by purchasing from non-sanctioned entities, industry sources told Reuters. Many of the July cargoes may also have been arranged during the window covered by the waiver.

The threat of punitive action has not gone away. A bill introduced in the US Senate on July 16 by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, would impose tariffs of up to 500% on countries that are among the top five purchasers of Russian crude. India, the world's third-largest oil importer, would almost certainly be targeted.

Saudi Arabia and UAE Find Workarounds

India's other major suppliers have adapted to the Hormuz disruption. Saudi Arabia has redirected most of its shipments through the Yanbu export terminal on the Red Sea, bypassing the strait entirely. India imported 403,000 bpd of Saudi crude in June via Yanbu, according to Reuters.

The UAE has relied on a pipeline to its Fujairah terminal and ship-to-ship transfers offshore Oman, east of the strait. UAE crude averaged 617,000 bpd in early July, making it India's second-largest supplier after Russia.

The Economic Toll

India's crude oil import bill surged 61% to $49.8 billion in the April-June quarter despite a 4% decline in volume, as Brent crude stayed above $100 per barrel for much of the period, according to data from the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell. The average import price swung from $114.48 per barrel in April to $83.22 in June as ceasefire signals eased prices.

Analysts warn that if the Hormuz disruption persists and Yemen's Houthi forces impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, India's dependence on Russian, West African and Latin American crude will only deepen — raising both logistical costs and diplomatic risks.
